newsitem.title: FRANCE: FRENCH GRAIN HARVEST BACK IN TOP GEAR AFTER RAIN.
newsitem.headline: FRENCH GRAIN HARVEST BACK IN TOP GEAR AFTER RAIN.

text.p: The French grain harvest is speeding north again after last week's punishing rain.
Combines were working two to three per field in the Seine-et-Marne district east of Paris on Monday to get the job done before the threat of further storms, crop experts said.

But fields in southern Picardie near Amiens, 120 km north of Paris, were too waterlogged to cope with machinery and farmers were left waiting for the soil to dry. The district was swamped with 110 millimetres of rain during the recent storms.
Weather office Meteo France predicted heavy weather and further storms on Monday, but for now these were mainly south of the capital where the wheat and barley harvest is over.
With most winter grain in store, France looks set to harvest less than the 34 million tonnes of soft wheat initially forecast this year but still above 33 million tonnes, crop analysts said.
That would be the second largest crop on record after last year's 34.7 million tonnes.
"It will be over 33 million tonnes unless there is a big surprise," one national crop official said.

But there were still very few indications on crop quality, one of the main headaches for millers after speculation gained ground that much of the crop would be suitable only for animal feed this year. Drought and then rain have interfered with normal growing cycles.
In high-yielding northern regions, rain has prevented a continuous harvest for the first time in several years. Farmers normally have a clear run at wheat and barley lasting five days.
The latest yield reports, however, were said to be less erratic than last year when productivity divided sharply into two zones.

France's 1996 wheat crop started off badly with mediocre yields in the Beauce bread-basket region south of Paris. But it got a huge lift from perfectly timed moisture as soon as the harvest had crossed the river Seine moving northwards.
Analysts said barley, especially spring varieties, was looking better than expected in some regions and predicted a French crop at or above last year's 9.5-9.6 million tonnes.
There had been fears of too much barley protein for use in malting, commanding a higher market value.
Crop officials, while stressing few laboratory tests were available, said some of the quality fears were now receding.
"It is far easier to assess the volume at this stage but people are a little less worried about the protein and quality than they were a few weeks ago," said one farm official.
South of Paris attention is swinging to maize, which lacked moisture for a while but has now benefited from rain.
Crop officials in the southwest said water was still needed in some localised areas where irrigation is still being rationed after a four-month drought between January and April.
Maize sowings rose one percent this year to 1.73 million hectares and a repeat of last year's yields would give France its second biggest maize crop, above 14.4 million tonnes.

In southern France, however, a post-harvest tally confirms significant drought damage to the specialist durum wheat crop, used for pasta and couscous. The early-harvested crop had none of the benefit of recent rain and is down by at least a quarter this year to some 900,000 tonnes, regional analysts said.
